Cc @Ivorforce @lawnjelly 

This should be interesting to profile. While it's not a priority for 4.5, it would be good for one of the three of us to get some preliminary understanding of where the issue is so we can come up with a proper plan of action for 4.6

_Godot 3.5.3_ _Godot master (4.5 beta 5ish)_ It looks like `GDScript::reload()` has changed a lot and is much more expensive than it was before. I confirmed that `GDScript::reload()` is called the same number of times during the loading process. So it seems like the ResourceLoader appears to be doing basically the same work between versions. Its not immediately obvious what the difference is since GDScript has changed so much. But it looks like the process of compiling GDScripts is just a lot slower than it used to be. It will require someone more familiar with GDScript to investigate further and confirm whether this increase in reload time is expected
Am afk at the moment but that looks like the 4.x gdscript optimizer taking some of the time, 3.x is unoptimized (until my pr) and certainly optmization might only be required for export.
Remember that the slow down appears also when the file is filled mostly with comments. That part should definitely be fixable. It sounds like the file may be unnecessarily re-parsed or something.

There is a significant difference between 4.x versions as well. Using the scene with one script I get the following (running through the editor):
- 4.2 ~80ms
- 4.3 ~70ms
- 4.4 ~130ms

So there was a performance regression along the way. Purely based on code I'm a bit suspicious about https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/96002 but haven't had time to confirm whether it is the one.

So with reverting [this code](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/96002/files#diff-2d47041c61b0e94d891650482b0cf9398f22729abdc811f94c2b7da902ed392fR883-R887) I see around a 40% speedup for loads when running from the editor. Worth noting though that this code is `#ifdef TOOLS_ENABLED` so it should be irrelevant for exported projects.

Due to the in editor load time regression mentioned above, I did another round of testing, this time in exported projects and I can't really reproduce *5 increase mentioned in the issue.

3.5.3: Single script: ~46, Two Scripts ~48
4.4.1: Single Script: ~70, Two Scripts ~80
- Binary tokenization does seem to have no significant influence for this MRP. The case might be different for scripts with many comments and empty lines though.
- Using official export templates
- Running on Fedora 42
- Having both exported projects on the same SSD

> In terms of real world numbers/impact, our game project sees a roughly 5x increase in purely loading time, from roughly 2 seconds in Godot 3.5.3, to roughly 10 seconds in Godot 4.4.1. These numbers are using exported versions of the game.

Given my results, I assume this is not about load time but about startup time? Godot 4.x startup needs longer than 3.x AFAIK, this is not directly linked with resource loading performance though.

> Given my results, I assume this is not about load time but about startup time? Godot 4.x startup needs longer than 3.x AFAIK, this is not directly linked with resource loading performance though.

No, this issue is purely related to `ResourceLoader.load()` time.
While start up time in general is worse in 4.4 (due to this and some other open issues), I've tried to isolate this issue to only focus on the actual `ResourceLoader.load()` time. Our actual game project's full "Start application to game fully loaded" is even worse than the ~5x stated in this issue, sadly 😅

The MRP does not showcase a ~5x increase, but our actual game project does. My understanding from rocket chat was that it was enough to showcase the regression happening, even if the MRP itself did not showcase the identical severity/impact as our actual game project.

We've measured a few different things (and across a few different machines), so to avoid any ambiguity, I ran some new tests now on my machine on our actual game project, with the following code:
```
var pre_time = Time.get_ticks_usec()
var resource = ResourceLoader.load(path)
var post_time = Time.get_ticks_usec()
var delta = post_time - pre_time
print("RL: %s usec (%s msec)" % [delta, delta / 1000])
```
Where `path` is the path to our main game scene.

System information again for easy reference: Windows 11 (build 26100) - Multi-window, 2 monitors - Vulkan (Forward+) - dedicated NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 (NVIDIA; 32.0.15.7283) - AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core Processor (24 threads)

3.5.3.stable, exported with default templates,  print output:
`RL: 1028802 usec (1028 msec)`

4.4.1.stable, exported with default templates, print output:
`RL: 4797690 usec (4797 msec)`

~4.7x increase in `ResourceLoader.load()` time.

In our actual game project, we have a **lot** of scripts referencing some very large scripts (analogous to the `HorribleScript.gd` in the MRP). My belief/hunch is that the largest factor for the `ResourceLoader.load()` increase comes from the re-parsing of this script several hundred times, which seems to be much heavier in 4.4 compared to 3.5 (as can be seen in the "Very Sad Example"s).
This hunch seems to be supported by the numbers I get if I add references to these very large scripts in existing scripts that do not currently have references to them, the load time increases slightly for every occurrence.

> My understanding from rocket chat was that it was enough to showcase the regression happening, even if the MRP itself did not showcase the identical severity/impact as our actual game project.

Yeah, not trying to invalidate the issue. It's just important to understand what's going on so I wanted to make sure.

Basically GDScript has become more complex since 3.x by doing more static typing related work. So some slowdown is expected. Let's say this is around the 2* slowdown we see in the single script scene. We might be able to optimize here but in general this slowdown is unavoidable due to new features.

The bigger problem seems to be the *1.2 slowdown between the scene with one and two scripts. The concerning thing is that based on your result this slowdown scales up with project complexity.

The MRP is just not ideal to test a solution for this, the complexity and slowdown for this case is too low, to verify a fix without running a lot of times.

If you are able to run a custom build of the engine it would be interesting to know how [this patch](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21706141/parser_cache_patch.txt) effects the slowdown in your complex project.
I'll see if I can get custom engine compile setup this evening and do a test of that patch. Will follow up in a few hours or so.

I can try to create an updated MRP. What should an updated MRP contain/show in order to be more helpful, if you have any thoughts on that?

> I can try to create an updated MRP. What should an updated MRP contain/show in order to be more helpful, if you have any thoughts on that?

It's hard to answer that without knowing what exactly is causing your main project to run so slow. 

The MRP should contain everything needed to reproduce the 5x performance regression and nothing else. Which is obviously totally vague, but without profiling your actual project, it's impossible for us to identify what the offending features are. 

That might mean it needs to have more scripts and more script interdependencies like it sounds like your game does. But it also might mean that you need to include other assets in addition to scripts.

New MRP setup

3 different `ResourceLoader.load()` scenarios:
* Happy: Loads a scene. Scene has a script. **Does NOT** reference the very expensive script.
* Sad: Loads a scene. Scene has a script. **DOES** reference the very expensive script
* Very sad: Loads a scene. Scene has a script. Scene also has 10 child nodes. Each child node has a (unique) script. All 11 scripts (1x loaded scene script + 10x unique child scripts) reference the same very expensive script.

Result:
3.5.3 Very Sad load duration is roughly 1.1x compared to Sad.
4.4.1 Very Sad load duration is roughly 4-5x compared to Sad.
4.4.1 Sad load duration is roughly 30% slower than 3.5.3. Might be expected due to GDScript changes.

---

Godot 3.5.3-stable vs Godot 4.4.1-stable
The following measurements are from same setup as before:
Windows 11 (build 26100) - Multi-window, 2 monitors - Vulkan (Forward+) - dedicated NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 (NVIDIA; 32.0.15.7283) - AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core Processor (24 threads)

Exported without debug, default templates.
Load durations are average of 5 runs, each run is start "game", press 1 of the load buttons. Close "game".


| Godot 3.5.3: Happy | Godot 3.5.3: Sad | Godot 3.5.3: Very Sad |
| --------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------ |
| 1 ms | 71 ms | 76 ms |

3.5.3 Very Sad load duration is roughly 1.1x compared to Sad.

| Godot 4.4.1: Happy | Godot 4.4.1: Sad | Godot 4.4.1: Very Sad |
| --------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------ |
 |  1 ms | 91 ms | 417 ms |

4.4.1 Very Sad load duration is roughly 4.5x compared to Sad.

Note: I also tried using `4.4.1-stable` manually compiled MSVC vs `4.4.1-stable + parse_cache_patch.txt` manually compiled MSVC, no meaningful difference compared to freshly downloaded 4.4.1-stable.

[ResourceLoader_3_5.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21708064/ResourceLoader_3_5.zip)
[ResourceLoader_4_4.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21708063/ResourceLoader_4_4.zip)

I repeatedly loaded the “very sad” scene using `CACHE_MODE_IGNORE_DEEP`, and the flame graph shows that `TextServer::spoof_check` takes about 24% of the time. This feature was introduced in #54905, with the milestone set to 4.0, so it should not exist in Godot 3. This could be part of the reason for the performance drop.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/10cbe8e6-f698-4088-bb6f-0fb096b73751)

With this check disable "very bad" scene loading time decreased from about 500ms to 400ms on my computer.

This check is guarded with `DEBUG_ENABLED` so it should not affect exported projects.

Even with the new MRP, when testing myself the patch lets bad and very bad load in the same time for me (this time running from editor).

When you tested the patch, did you correctly build and configure a custom export template?

> When you tested the patch, did you correctly build and configure a custom export template?

I did not know I needed to create a custom export template. I thought it was enough to custom compile & build normally using the manually compiled editor binary. My apologies, I'm still new to custom compiling Godot.

For future reference, are custom export templates always required to test the a project, either via editor or after export?

---

With `parser_cache_patch.txt` **correctly** applied, it seems that this is indeed fixed!
In the MRP, 4.4.1 load duration drops from ~420 ms to ~105 ms. It's ever so slightly above the single scene scenario, but to a negligible degree.
In our actual game project, the load duration drops from ~4800 ms to ~1500 ms. While still a ~50% increase from 3.5.3, this is vastly improved.

> For future reference, are custom export templates always required to test the a project, either via editor or after export?

You can think of the compiled engine as a runtime that executes the project. When building yourself you will have to make sure, that the runtime running the project is compiled with the changes. When running from editor the runtime which also powers the editor is used so compiling the editor with a patch is enough. But when exporting, Godot bundles a runtime from the export templates with the project so the exported project uses a runtime from the templates. So when testing an exported project you need to build a custom export template.

---

My fazit:
- To decrease load time of complex scenes and script we should look into caching parsers for the duration of the whole load. (Or rework the analyzer to use shallow scripts where possible and don't parse when there is a cached shallow script, but the regression potential is probably very high.)
- To decrease load time when started from editor: Only run `update_exports` when the editor hint is set, or optimize `update_exports` to reuse the parse results from `reload`.
- Some speedup in the parser/analyzer process should also be possible. E.g. avoiding expensive text server calls that are only used for editor warnings.

> > For future reference, are custom export templates always required to test the a project, either via editor or after export?
> 
> You can think of the compiled engine as a runtime that executes the project. When building yourself you will have to make sure, that the runtime running the project is compiled with the changes. When running from editor the runtime which also powers the editor is used so compiling the editor with a patch is enough. But when exporting, Godot bundles a runtime from the export templates with the project so the exported project uses a runtime from the templates. So when testing an exported project you need to build a custom export template.

Thanks for explaining!

To clarify something regarding the parser cache patch, would this be suitable for us to use in production for our project (i.e. using a custom compiled release template)? Or is it more a proof of concept that shouldn't be used in production due to adverse side-effects, and we should instead wait for a proper PR that deals with the bullet points you listed at the end of your post?
Asking since if the timeline for a proper fix is 4.6, that's a long time for our project.

The patch is a prove of concept that caches parse trees for the entire runtime of the program. It's not suited for production since it might increase the memory usage of a complex project significantly. I'm also not sure how thread safe it is, so please don't use it!

@lantanadan This is a different issue from the OP, do you mind making a dedicated issue report? Its pretty clear your issue has to do with the fullscreen mode while this issue is about a specific performance regression when comparing 4.x to 3.x that is explained by the GDScript compiler.

Its pretty clear your issue has to do with the fullscreen mode while this issue is about a specific performance regression when comparing 4.x to 3.x that is explained by the GDScript compiler.

I'm happy to move this post to a separate thread if this issue is found to be completely unrelated. My instinct was that my issue could shed some light on where the threaded performance regressions came from or at least potentially point OP and crew in the right direction.
